title: The Reinvestment Blind Spot: Why a Not-for-Profit's Commercial Arm Rarely Keeps What It Earns
linkedin:
A profitable trading arm inside a not-for-profit is rarely the problem we see. What happens to the surplus afterwards usually is.

World Humanitarian Day fell on 19 August, a good prompt to notice how many not-for-profits now run a genuine commercial arm alongside the mission, an op shop, a training division, a cafe, a consulting arm.

The pattern across these trading businesses is not that they lose money. Most trade profitably, sometimes more consistently than the mission side of the organisation ever manages. But the surplus rarely stays where it was earned. The moment a good year is reported, it gets swept into program spending, and the commercial arm starts the next year with exactly the working capital it had twelve months earlier, even though the business it needs to run has grown.

Over a few good years that becomes a real ceiling. The trading arm cannot open a second shop, add a training cohort or take on a bigger contract, because every dollar it made has already gone to a program before the next opportunity turns up. Growth then has to be funded by a fresh grant application or appeal instead of reinvested profit, which is slower and far less certain.

None of this argues for spending less on the mission. It argues for deciding, deliberately, what share of a strong trading year gets reinvested before the rest is allocated to programs.

Full piece on the ProfitPulse blog.

The pattern worth a closer look is what happens to that surplus once the year closes. In many organisations it gets allocated to programs straight away, which is a reasonable instinct, but it also means the trading arm starts the next year with exactly the working capital it had twelve months earlier. Over a few strong years that becomes a genuine ceiling on how much the commercial side can grow, and expansion ends up depending on the next grant round rather than the profit already earned.
